articles.title: New expert consensus highlights the role of circadian rhythms in treating bipolar disorder
articles.summary: Growing evidence suggests that disruptions in circadian rhythms play a significant role in bipolar disorder. Now, researchers have developed a framework for using light, dark, and daily routines to help stabilize mood and improve sleep.

articles.title: The hidden business of the submissive internet “tradwife”
articles.summary: A new study dissects the internet "tradwife" trend, revealing how popular influencers use vintage aesthetics to sell a return to patriarchal gender roles. Behind the homemade bread, these creators are running lucrative digital marketing businesses.

articles.title: Eating within 8 hours may help keep the aging brain sharp
articles.summary: Eating within a shorter daily window may help protect certain thinking skills as people age. In a small six-month trial, older women who limited eating to about 8 to 9 hours a day performed better on planning and problem-solving tests than those who ate over 12 hours. Both groups lost similar amounts of weight, hinting that when people eat could matter in addition to how much they eat.

articles.title: Your dreams aren’t random. Your brain is rewriting reality
articles.summary: Dreams are not random mental noise. A large study of more than 3,700 dream and waking reports found that what we experience during sleep is shaped by both our personalities and the world around us. Rather than simply replaying daily events, the dreaming brain mixes memories, emotions, imagined possibilities, and familiar settings into vivid new scenarios.

articles.title: ADHD might remain underdiagnosed in England despite recent surge in recorded cases
articles.summary: A new analysis of millions of medical records reveals that ADHD remains heavily underdiagnosed in England. Despite a recent spike in recognized cases, diagnosis rates fall far below global estimates, particularly among middle-aged and older adults.

articles.title: New research sheds light on how feeling forgiven by God shapes relationship repair
articles.summary: A new diary study of cohabiting couples reveals that when individuals feel a sense of spiritual forgiveness from a higher power, they are more likely to make amends and forgive their partners after an everyday relationship conflict.

articles.title: The psychology of jealousy: Study explores how perceived mate value is linked to relationship conflict
articles.summary: People in open relationships often experience less jealousy than monogamous couples. However, a new study reveals that feeling less attractive than your partner still sparks conflict in both relationship types, highlighting the deep roots of romantic insecurity.

articles.title: A hidden Alzheimer’s tipping point may decide who gets dementia
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a possible tipping point that helps determine whether Alzheimer’s-related brain changes lead to dementia. The key may lie in how the brain’s immune cells respond to plaques and tau, offering a promising new target for treatments designed to extend cognitive resilience.

articles.title: Inside the Backrooms: The internet’s creepiest place is becoming a tourist attraction
articles.summary: The Backrooms began as a single eerie image of empty yellow rooms, but internet users transformed it into a vast fictional world that feels disturbingly real. Through videos, games, maps, survival guides and social media stories, audiences do more than watch the horror unfold. They help build and explore it. Researchers suggest this popularity reflects a new kind of digital tourism, where people emotionally enter imaginary places filled with mystery, nostalgia and unease.

articles.title: Oral GLP-1 drugs may quiet the brain’s food craving circuit
articles.summary: Newer oral drugs related to semaglutide medications such as Ozempic reduced pleasure-driven eating in mice by quieting a deep brain reward circuit. The finding could open new avenues for understanding food cravings and potentially treating substance use disorder.

articles.title: A single dose reversed autism-like symptoms in adult mice within hours
articles.summary: Even mild inflammation during pregnancy led mouse offspring to develop persistent brain overactivity, sensory sensitivity, repetitive behaviors, and increased seizure risk. Remarkably, one dose of rapamycin improved nearly all of these problems within about two hours. The benefits were temporary, but they suggest that adult brain circuits may remain far more adaptable than previously believed.
